| [NOTE-888](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-888.md) | Athanassoulis et al. — Designing access methods: the RUM conjecture | The paper names three per-operation overheads of an access method, each a ratio to the base data alone (read, update and space amplification, each minimum 1.0), and conjectures that bounding any two forces a lower bound on the third. The extremes themselves show the overheads are not symmetric: the space-minimal design is also update-minimal, and the read-minimal design keeps updates at 2.0, so the clean conflicts are read against space and update against both. Build cost appears in the table but is outside the triangle, there is no workload weighting, no time or deadline, and no cost of examining an item other than reading it. | Read |
| [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md) | Gupta — Selection of views to materialize in a data warehouse | Gupta states view selection on general AND-OR view graphs as minimizing frequency-weighted query cost plus update-frequency-weighted maintenance cost under a space budget. | [NOTE-890](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-890.md) | Gupta & Mumick — Selection of views to materialize under a maintenance cost constraint | Gupta and Mumick choose views to materialize so as to minimize frequency-weighted query cost subject to a cap S on total maintenance time, the sum over chosen views of update frequency times a per-update maintenance cost that depends on which other views are stored. Because storing one view can make another cheaper to maintain, benefit per unit of maintenance is not monotone and the single-view greedy of earlier work can be arbitrarily bad. For OR view graphs (each view computed from one other, as in data cubes) a greedy that adds whole "inverted tree sets" gets at least 1 − 1/e (63%) of the benefit of an optimal solution that may use as much maintenance as the greedy did, the greedy using up to 2S, assuming no inverted-tree piece of the optimum alone exceeds S (Theorem 1, unproved here); without that assumption it gets half the optimum's benefit per unit of maintenance (Theorem 2). Each greedy stage enumerates exponentially many sets in general; for general AND-OR graphs there is only an exact A* search with exponential worst case. Upkeep is a budget, not a term traded against query savings; build cost, storage and staleness are not modelled, and the experiments are on random graphs of 10 to 25 nodes. | Read |
| [NOTE-891](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-891.md) | Yao — Should tables be sorted? | For storing a set of n keys from a universe {1,…,m} in a table so that the membership query (is x in S?) is answered with the fewest worst-case adaptive probes, Yao proves that when the table cells may hold only keys of S or a bounded number of pointer symbols, sorted order with binary search (⌈lg(n+1)⌉ probes) is optimal once m exceeds a Ramsey-number threshold N(n, p, q), whatever the arrangement rule, table size or hashing scheme. | [NOTE-893](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-893.md) | Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph & Sleator — Competitive snoopy caching | For a shared-bus multiprocessor whose caches can either keep a replicated block (and pay one bus cycle for every write to it) or drop it (and pay p to fetch it again if it is read), the paper gives counter-based on-line algorithms whose total bus cost on every request sequence is at most twice that of the best off-line algorithm, and proves that no deterministic on-line algorithm can guarantee better than 2. The rule is: drop a copy once the writes it has caused since it was last read have cost as much as refetching it. With a third option (reading or writing through without fetching) the lower bound rises to 3, and the algorithm given is 3-competitive ignoring writebacks, 4 counting them; with associative caches the bound becomes the paging ratio. The paper never names rent-or-buy or ski rental; its rent is upkeep paid on an idle copy, and its purchase is the refetch after dropping, the reverse orientation of building a bin. A query carries a precision constraint R, and the system chooses which values to fetch exactly so that the answer interval is at most R wide whatever the true values, at least total refresh cost. For SUM (and AVG without a predicate) that choice is a 0/1 knapsack problem, NP-complete in general and polynomial with equal costs; COUNT and MIN have simple rules. Staleness becomes bounded imprecision, never error, and the cost of the source-side upkeep that guarantees this, and of setting the bound widths, is outside the optimization. The one experiment is 90 stock prices with random costs. | Read |
| [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md) | Fagin, Lotem & Naor — Optimal aggregation algorithms for middleware | Given m lists of the same N objects, each sorted by one attribute's grade, and a monotone function combining the grades, the threshold algorithm (TA) reads the lists in parallel, random-accesses each newly seen object's other grades, and stops once k seen objects score at least the combined score of the last grades read. It is correct for every monotone combining function, needs constant buffers, and is instance optimal among correct algorithms that make no "wild guesses": on every database its cost is within a constant factor of any such algorithm's, the factor being m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, which is best possible when the combining function is strict (conjunction-like). Without the no-wild-guesses restriction no algorithm is instance optimal, and the counterexample is a two-list conjunction whose target sits in the middle of both lists, which any algorithm must search linearly. Fagin's Algorithm's sublinear cost O(N^((m−1)/m) k^(1/m)) is cited from Fagin, not proved here, and holds only when the lists' orderings are probabilistically independent. The model prices queries over a given set of single-attribute sorted lists. It does not price building or keeping the lists, choosing an arrangement, or any computation beyond accesses. | Read |
